content: During the meeting, it was determined that the Evidence Review Group (ERG), a large international group with members from various countries, would actively contribute to the development of recommendations. Members of the Methodology Group (MG) presented evidence profiles and evidence-to-recommendation tables, which included data on benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, resource use, and feasibility. Regarding patient values and preferences, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) agreed that the evidence could be applied universally across all recommendations. Qualitative studies indicated that women may experience fear and anxiety related to screening, colposcopy, or treatment, and may feel burdened by the need for a second visit for treatment. However, once women decide to undergo screening, they generally find the tests and immediate treatment acceptable. Systematic reviews showed that women who test positive for CIN 1 prefer more frequent screening and active management. Controlled trials demonstrated that women find cryotherapy and LEEP (loop electrosurgical excision procedure) acceptable and are satisfied with a screen-and-treat approach. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a cervical cancer prevention and control costing tool, which includes modules for estimating the costs of HPV vaccination and screen-and-treat programs. This tool is designed to assist program managers in budgeting for these interventions. The cost data for each intervention were collected from various countries, and calculation tables were created. This information, along with the expertise of ERG members, was critical in discussing the resources required for each strategy. The GDG and ERG made recommendations by weighing the overall desirable and undesirable consequences of screen-and-treat strategies, considering important outcomes, patient values and preferences, resource use, feasibility, and the certainty of the evidence. Eight WHO guidelines for screening and treating precancerous cervical lesions were developed through consensus and unanimous voting, with no major disagreements noted during the April 2012 meeting. Recommendations were classified as either strong or conditional based on the WHO handbook for guideline development. Strong recommendations were phrased as we recommend, indicating that the net desirable consequences of the strategy clearly outweighed the alternatives. Conditional recommendations were phrased as we suggest, reflecting less certainty about the net benefits. The WHO screen-and-treat strategies underwent a rigorous peer review process. Questions for guideline development were circulated among the WHO Steering Group and GDG, and once agreed upon, were sent to the ERG. The protocol for systematic reviews was also shared with the GDG and discussed during an ERG meeting, which included representatives from the European Guidelines Development Group. Regular discussions and conference calls were held with the GDG to review data from literature, models, and estimated parameters. The final draft guidelines were reviewed by GDG members before WHO clearance. Strong recommendations imply that most individuals in the given situation would want the recommended course of action, while conditional recommendations acknowledge that many individuals may choose alternative options. For clinicians, strong recommendations suggest that most patients should receive the intervention, whereas conditional recommendations require clinicians to help patients make decisions consistent with their values and preferences. Decision aids may be useful in these cases. Policymaking for conditional recommendations often involves substantial debate and stakeholder involvement. The guidelines emphasize targeting women aged 30 years and older for screening, as they are at higher risk for cervical cancer. Priority should be given to screening women aged 30–49 years rather than maximizing the number of lifetime screenings. Even a single lifetime screening can be beneficial. Screening intervals may vary based on financial and infrastructural resources. For HIV-positive women or those in high HIV-endemic areas, screening should begin as soon as they test positive for HIV. Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) is appropriate for women with visible transformation zones, typically those younger than 50 years, as menopause often causes the transformation zone to recede into the endocervical canal. Cryotherapy is the first-choice treatment for screen-positive women eligible for this procedure. If cryotherapy is not suitable, LEEP is the alternative. Eligibility for cryotherapy requires that the entire lesion and the squamocolumnar junction are visible, and the lesion does not cover more than 75% of the ectocervix. If the lesion extends beyond the cryoprobe or into the endocervical canal, LEEP is recommended. All screen-positive women should undergo visual inspection with acetic acid to determine eligibility for cryotherapy and rule out large lesions or suspected cervical cancer. VIA should be performed by trained providers. In HPV test-based screen-and-treat strategies, HPV-negative women are not treated, while HPV-positive women are treated based on VIA eligibility for cryotherapy or LEEP. In the HPV test followed by VIA strategy, HPV-positive women undergo VIA as a second screening test to determine treatment eligibility. HPV-positive and VIA-positive women are treated, while HPV-positive and VIA-negative women are not. Screening intervals for women who test negative on VIA or cytology should be every three to five years. For women who test negative on an HPV test, rescreening should occur after a minimum of five years. Women who have received treatment should undergo post-treatment follow-up screening at one year to ensure treatment effectiveness. The expert panel strongly recommends against using cold knife conization (CKC) as a treatment in screen-and-treat strategies due to greater associated harms compared to cryotherapy or LEEP, despite similar benefits. This recommendation applies regardless of HIV status. The panel suggests using HPV testing and cryotherapy (or LEEP) over VIA and cryotherapy (or LEEP) where resources permit, as HPV testing offers greater reductions in cervical cancer and related mortality. However, in resource-constrained settings, VIA and cryotherapy (or LEEP) may be preferred. These recommendations apply to women regardless of HIV status. The panel also suggests HPV testing and cryotherapy (or LEEP) over cytology followed by colposcopy and cryotherapy (or LEEP), as HPV testing offers slightly greater reductions in cancer and mortality. However, cytology programs require more resources for quality control, training, and waiting times, and colposcopy necessitates a second visit. In countries with high-quality cytology-based screening programs, either HPV testing or cytology followed by colposcopy may be used.
